9:16: The Lord is speaking of the people of Ephraim as if they were a plant whose root has dried up and that will not produce fruit. He means they will have no children or prosperity.
Here, womb represents the act of giving birth to children.
10:1: The speaker is speaking as if Israel were an emptying vine, a productive plant that spreads out and bears fruit. He means that the nation had grown and become prosperous.
The speaker continues to speak as if Israel were a vine that places fruit for himself. He means that the people used their growing prosperity for their own benefit.
10:2: Here the heart represents where the people’s motives and intentions exist. By describing it as if it were slippery, the speaker shows that their motives and intensions were insincere and deceitful, as they were divided in their devotion to the Lord.
10:3: The people are using the question form to emphasize that a king could do nothing at all to help them.
10:4: The point of this comparison is that just as a poisonous weed grows quickly and spreads harm everywhere, so does the judgment that the people produce.
The speaker is using cutting a covenant as a common expression of his culture to mean they are making or establishing a covenant.
10:5: The speaker is calling the city of Bethel Beth Aven as a derogatory wordplay because of all the idol worship there.
The word translated as will shout normally refers to a shout of joy. But here, the shout is not one of joy but one of fear.
10:6: The word Yareb represents the written Hebrew text both here and in 5:13. See what you decided to do there.
10:7: The point of this comparison is that just as a splinter on the face of the waters is small and helplessly carried away by the force of the water, so the king of Samaria will be swept away and come to nothing.
Here, the face of the waters represents the surface of the water.
10:8: The word Aven is a shortened version of “Beth Aven” (which means “house of evil”) mentioned in verse 5 and refers to the city of Bethel.
The terms Thorn and thistle mean similar things. The speaker is using the two terms together for emphasis.
וְאָמְרוּ לֶהָרִים כַּסּוּנוּ וְלַגְּבָעוֹת נִפְלוּ עָלֵינוּ
The people are speaking to the mountains and the hills, which they know cannot hear them. They are doing this to express that they feel very strongly about their desire to escape the Lord’s judgment.
10:9: The speaker is speaking of Israel persisting in their sin as if the Israelites had stood still in the place where their sin began.
The speaker is using the question form to emphasize that war will certainly be the consequence of their sinfulness.
The speaker is using son of as a common expression of the culture to indicate people who have a certain characteristic. In this case, the people of Gibeah are characterized by doing what is unjust.
10:10: The phrase to their two eyes is a translation of the written Hebrew text. Later Hebrew scribes, however, have recommended in the margin of the text what they considered to be a correction, by changing one letter.
10:11: The Lord is speaking as if Ephraim were a trained heifer, a young cow that had been taught to work. He means that the people of Ephraim had become accustomed to easy, pleasant labor.

The Lord is speaking as if he would lay a yoke on a work animal when he says that he passed over upon the goodness of her neck. He means that he will subject the people of Ephraim to hard labor and suffering.
אַרְכִּיב אֶפְרַיִם יַחֲרוֹשׁ יְהוּדָה יְשַׂדֶּד־לוֹ יַעֲקֹב
The Lord is speaking as if the people were work animals that he would harness to plow and harrow the fields. He means that he will subject Ephraim, Judah, and Jacob to hard toil.
10:12: The Lord is speaking as if righteousness were a crop that the people should Sow and then reap. He means that they should do what is right and so receive the Lord’s covenant faithfulness in return.
The Lord is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
The Lord is speaking as if the people needed to Till for yourselves tillage, breaking up new ground. He means that they should make a thorough change in the way they live.
The Lord is speaking of the Lord’s abundant blessing as if he rains it down on the people like water from the sky.
10:13: Hosea is speaking as if wickedness and injustice were crops that the people had plowed and reaped. He means that the people did evil and then experienced its harmful consequences.
The Lord is speaking as if the people’s deception were fruit that they had eaten. He means that the people have experienced the harmful consequences of their lies and deceit.
10:15: Here, Bethel represents the people who live in Bethel.
11:1: The Lord is speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were a young child here and in the next few verses.
The Lord is speaking of the nation of Israel as if it were his son.
11:2: The phrase They called to them is a translation of the written Hebrew text. It is unclear who They would refer to.
Here the phrase from their faces could: (1) represent “from their presence,” referring to the prophets of the Lord.
The phrase from their faces is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense.
11:3: The Lord is speaking of his early care for the people of Ephraim as if he as a parent had been teaching a small child and taught Ephraim to walk.

The phrase He took them upon his arms could be translated to mean: (1) that the Lord picked up Ephraim, pictured as a small child, and carried him in his arms. It may be that Hosea is speaking about the Lord here, or it may be that the original reading continued the Lord’s speech in the first person, as the ancient Greek and Syriac translations have it; or (2) that the Lord took Ephraim, pictured as a small child, and held onto Ephraim’s arms as the Lord taught Ephraim to walk.
The Lord is speaking of caring for the people of Israel as if he healed them from sickness.
11:4: The Lord is speaking of the kind and gentle ways he led the people of Israel as if they were cords of humanity and bands of love by which he drew them along.
וָאֶהְיֶה לָהֶם כִּמְרִימֵי עֹל עַל לְחֵיהֶם

The phrase And I was to them like the lifters of a yoke on their jaws is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. A yoke is never placed on an animal’s jaws, but on the animal’s neck. Further, if this were an image of release from slavery, it would describe lifting the yoke from the animal, not lifting it on the animal. It seems that the word translated as yoke should be pronounced with a different vowel, which would then be the word for “infant.” The word translated as jaws also means “cheek.” Therefore, this could mean: (1) the Lord is continuing the picture of Ephraim as a small child and describing his tender care for them.
The Lord is speaking of his care for the people of Israel as if he were a parent who bent down and fed a small child.
11:5: The implication is that they refused to return to worshiping the Lord.
11:6: The Lord assumes that readers will know the bars being referred to are part of the city gates.
The Lord is speaking of the destruction that the sword will cause as if the sword would devour its victims like an animal eating its prey.
11:7: The Lord is speaking of his people abandoning their loyalty to him as if they were physically turning away from him to walk in a different direction.
11:8: The Lord is using the question form to express the anguish and reluctance he feels at the thought of giving up his people.
The Lord is using the question form to express how unwilling he is to destroy his people as he destroyed Admah.

The point of this comparison is that while the cities of Admah and Zeboiim were completely destroyed (see Deuteronomy 29:23), this is something that the Lord does not want to do to the people of Israel.
The Lord is speaking of the turmoil of his strong feelings of anguish as if his heart were physically turned over within him.
Here the Lord speaks of his heart as it represents where his feelings and desires exist.
11:10: The point of this comparison is that just as a lion roars loudly and powerfully, so the Lord will summon his people with a loud, powerful voice.
The Lord is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were his sons returning to their father.
11:11: The point of this comparison is that just as a bird would be timid, fearful, and trembling in response to a lion’s roar, so the people of Israel will hurry back from exile with respectful fear when the Lord summons them to return.
The point of this comparison is that just as a dove is gentle and docile, so the people of Israel will come back without objections from the land of Assyria, ready to obey the Lord.
11:12: The Lord is speaking of the constant lying of the people of Ephraim as if they had surrounded me with lies on every side.

Here, house means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So the house of Israel figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel.
וִיהוּדָה עֹד רָד עִם־אֵל וְעִם־קְדוֹשִׁים נֶאֱמָן

The sentence But Judah still roams with God, and is established with the Holy One could mean: (1) that although Israel is far from God, Judah is still following him. This could be possible because the word is plural, but words for God are often plural to indicate his majesty.
12:1: אֶפְרַיִם רֹעֶה רוּחַ וְרֹדֵף קָדִים כָּל־הַיּוֹם
These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
The speaker is speaking of Ephraim’s useless pursuit foreign alliances as if it were feeding on wind and pursuing the east-wind, an activity that gains nothing real.
The speaker says all the day as a generalization for emphasis.

The speaker is using cut a covenant as a common expression of his culture which means “to make” or “establish” a covenant. Here it refers to agreements that Israel made when they forsook the help that their God offered to pursue help from enemy nations.
12:2: The implication is that dispute here refers to a formal legal complaint, as when one party brings a lawsuit against another.
The speaker is speaking of how Jacob has lived as if it were the paths or ways that he usually walks along.
12:3: This refers to the account of Jacob’s birth described in Genesis 25:26, when he came out of the womb grasping the heel of his twin brother Esau.
This and the first line of the next verse refer to the account described in Genesis 32:22-32, when Jacob wrestled with an angel who turned out to be God.
12:4: This refers to the event described in Genesis 32:28-30 when God revealed himself to Jacob at Bethel and spoke with him.
The phrase with us is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense, since God spoke to Jacob at Bethel, not to his descendants.
12:6: The speaker is speaking of repenting and turning back to God as if the people had been walking one direction and must instead return to him.

The phrase by your God could mean: (1) that the Israelites should return to God by following his ways, as described in the rest of the verse; or (2) that the Israelites should rely on God’s help to empower them to return.
12:7: The implication is that the merchant here stands for the tradesmen of Ephraim, whom the speaker is portraying as dishonest traders.
Here, his hand represents his possession and control of the scales.

Here, scales describes an instrument for determining the weight of an object. It consists of a central post with a crossbar from which two pans are hung. An object may be placed in one pan and known weights placed in the other pan until the crossbar remains level, indicating that both pans contain an equal weight. By using incorrect weights these merchants were deceiving those with whom they traded in order to increase their wealth.
12:8: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
12:9: The Lord is speaking of bringing the people back to humble dependence on him as if it were making them dwell in tents again.
The Lord assumes that readers will know that the exodus is meant when he mentions the land of Egypt.
The Lord is using the term as in the days to refer to a specific time.

The implication is that the appointed festival refers to the Festival of Shelters, during which the people lived in tents as temporary shelters to remember how their ancestors lived in the wilderness after leaving Egypt.
12:10: Here, the hand of the prophets represents the prophets as the agents through whom the Lord acted.
12:11: Here, Gilead represents the people of Gilead.
The implication is that the people of Gilead were well known for their idolatry and violent deeds.
The implication is that Gilgal was a place of pagan worship, so the people’s sacrificing there was offensive to the Lord rather than pleasing to him.
Here, In Gilgal represents the people who lived in Gilgal.

The point of this comparison is that just as heaps of stones cleared onto the furrows of a plowed field are nothing but useless piles of rubble, so their altars will be torn down into ruined heaps of stone.
12:12: This refers to the occasion described in Genesis 27:43 when Jacob fled to Aram (in the land of Haran) in order to escape from his brother Esau.

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional.
12:13: וּבְנָבִיא הֶעֱלָה יְהוָה אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמִּצְרָיִם וּבְנָבִיא
The speaker assumes that readers will know that the prophet through whom the Lord brought Israel up from Egypt was Moses.
12:14: The speaker is speaking of his Lord repaying Ephraim for his shameful conduct as if the reproach were an object that the Lord could return to him.
13:1: Here, Ephraim represents the people who were leaders of the northern kingdom of Israel, since Ephraim was its largest and most prominent tribe.
The speaker is speaking of people exalting themselves and being proud or arrogant as if they had physically lifted up themselves.

The implication is that, by worshiping Baal, the people of Ephraim brought about their own destruction as a nation, as if they had died. Their disobedience would eventually lead to the end of the nation of Israel.
13:3: The point of this comparison is that just as a cloud and the dew that appears early in the day disappears as the day goes on, so the people of Ephraim will soon disappear.
The point of this comparison is that just as chaff is quickly blown away from the threshing floor and is worthless, so the people of Ephraim will be swept away.
The point of this comparison is that just as smoke quickly dissipates as it goes out from a window, so the people of Ephraim will soon disappear.
13:6: The Lord is speaking of the provision he gave the people as if it were pasturage where they fed like animals and became satisfied.
The Lord is speaking of the people becoming proud as if their heart were lifted up.
13:7: The point of this comparison is that just as a lion attacks its prey fiercely, so the Lord will act fiercely toward the people in judgment.
The point of this comparison is that just as a leopard lurks beside the path to ambush its prey, so the Lord will watch and wait for the right time to bring judgment on them.
13:8: The point of this comparison is that just as a bereaved bear attacks with ferocious rage when someone takes her cubs, so the Lord will confront the people in his anger.
The Lord is speaking of destroying the people as if he were a wild animal that would tear open the enclosure of their heart.
The point of this comparison is that just as a lioness devours its prey, so the Lord will completely destroy the people.
13:9: Here, Israel represents the people of the northern kingdom of Israel.
13:10: The Lord is using the question form to emphasize that the people’s king is unable to save them.
13:12: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
The speaker is speaking of all of Ephraim’s sinfulness as if it were a physical object that is bound up and stored up to be kept for the future.
13:13: The speaker is speaking of the suffering that judgment will bring on the people as if it were pains of a woman giving birth.
13:14: Here, hand represents the power or grip of Sheol, the place of the dead.
אֱהִי דְבָרֶיךָ מָוֶת אֱהִי קָטָבְךָ שְׁאוֹל
The Lord is speaking to Death and Sheol, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly that they deserve death.
אֱהִי דְבָרֶיךָ מָוֶת אֱהִי קָטָבְךָ שְׁאוֹל
The meaning of these two questions could be: (1) that the Lord is calling on Death to bring out its plagues and for Sheol to bring out its destructive forces.

Here the Lord is speaking as if his Relenting toward Israel were a thing that could be hidden from my eyes, out of his sight so that he could not act on it. He means that he will not change his mind and show mercy to Israel.
13:15: The speaker is speaking of Ephraim prospering more than the other tribes as if he were a plant that bears fruit.
The speaker is speaking of the destructive judgment of the enemies from the east that the Lord will send, the wind of the Lord, as if it were an easterly, a scorching wind from the east.

These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional.

The word translated as will be ashamed is a translation of the written Hebrew text. This reading, however, does not seem to make sense. Scholars suggest that two letters got switched from the original reading, which was the word meaning “will dry up.” The ancient Greek and Syriac translations also translated the word as “will dry up.”
13:16: Here, Samaria represents the people who live in the city of Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom.
Here, the sword represents warfare and violent death in battle.
14:1: The speaker is speaking to the Israelites as if they had physically been walking away but could Return to walk back to the Lord. He means that they should repent of living in ways that are displeasing to the Lord and instead live in the manner in which the Lord wants people to live.
The speaker is speaking of the ruin that the people’s sin has brought upon them as if they had physically stumbled.
14:2: Here the people are speaking of the Lord forgiving their sins as if they were a mark that he could erase or take away.

The phrase and let us repay with bulls of our lips is a translation of the written Hebrew text, which compares a sincere prayer of obedience to the sacrifice of a bull (see chapter 6:6). The ancient Greek translation, however, understood the word translated as “bulls” to be the word for “fruit.” Several modern translations follow this reading.
Here, bulls of our lips represents the words of praise and the vows that the people offer to the Lord in place of animal sacrifices.
14:3: In this context, horse represent military strength so the people are saying they will not rely on military strength. Here the word horse is singular in form, but it refers to all horses as a group.
Here, the work of our hands represents the idols that the people have made with their hands.
14:4: The Lord is speaking of forgiving the people and restoring their previous relationship as if he would heal them from a sickness.
The Lord is speaking of the people’s abandonment of worshiping him to worshiping idols as if it were a physical turning away from following him.
The Lord is using my nose as part of a common expression of this culture, “the burning of his nose” which means that the Lord is angry.
Here the Lord is speaking of his anger as if it had been moving toward them but now has turned away from them.
14:5: The point of this comparison is that just as the dew brings moisture and life to plants, so the Lord will bring nourishment and new life to Israel.
The point of this comparison is that just as the lily blossoms with beauty, so the people of Israel will flourish and grow.
The point of this comparison is that just as the great trees of Lebanon send down deep, firm roots, so the people of Israel will become strong and firmly established.
14:6: The Lord is speaking of the people of Israel as if they were a plant whose shoots spread out and grow. He means that they will increase in influence and prosperity.
The point of this comparison is that just as the olive tree is beautiful and majestic, so the people of Israel will be splendid.
The point of this comparison is that just as the cedar forests of Lebanon give off a pleasant fragrance, so the people of Israel will be pleasing and delightful.
14:7: Here the speaker is speaking of the people of Israel resuming a right relationship with the Lord as if they would return to a place from which they had gone away.
The speaker is speaking of the Lord’s protection as if it were a shadow in which people could dwell and find shelter.
The point of this comparison is that just as the vine produces an abundant harvest, so the people of Israel will flourish and multiply.
The point of this comparison is that just as the wine of Lebanon was famous and highly valued, so His remembrance will be renowned.
14:8: The Lord is using the question form to state emphatically that he wants nothing more to do with idols.
As throughout the book of Hosea, Ephraim, the name of the largest of the northern tribes, represents the entire northern kingdom of Israel.

The Lord is using what to me as a common expression of the culture to mean “I have nothing to do with.” the Lord is expressing that he is disgusted by the people of Ephraim mixing idol worship with worship of the Lord.
The point of this comparison is that just as a luxuriant cypress stays green and provides shade and shelter, so the Lord continually provides for and protects his people.
The Lord is speaking of the blessings and prosperity that he gives to his people as if they were fruit that comes from him.
14:9: מִי חָכָם וְיָבֵן אֵלֶּה נָבוֹן וְיֵדָעֵם
The speaker is using the question form to challenge his readers to be wise and Discerning enough to understand and heed his message.

The speaker is speaking of how the Lord wants people to live as if it were the ways of the Lord, that is, paths to walk on. He speaks of obeying the Lord as the righteous will walk on these paths and of disobeying as stumbling on them.
